query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A thermally activated oxide tribofilm forms on FeNiCrCoCu during sliding at high temperature and serves as the primary mechanism governing both wear resistance and near-surface plastic deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy thin coating on a steel substrate, produced under standard atmospheric conditions.
generation.intervention: Vary the oxygen partial pressure in the sliding environment (from near-zero to ambient or higher) while keeping other test parameters constant.
generation.conditions: High-temperature (800–900 °C) sliding tests with controlled load and speed in environments of differing oxygen levels.
generation.structural_mediator: The growth and stability of a protective oxide tribofilm on the coating surface.
generation.mechanism: Under higher oxygen partial pressure, a stable oxide tribofilm prevents direct metal–metal contact, reducing friction and mitigating plastic deformation at the interface.
generation.predicted_outcome: Increasing oxygen partial pressure lowers wear rates and dislocation activity; suppressing oxygen availability leads to higher wear and more severe deformation.
generation.baseline: An as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating tested at 800–900 °C under ambient air conditions provides reference wear and deformation data.
generation.boundary: Above 900 °C or at extreme sliding speeds, oxide spallation or diffusion-driven changes may overwhelm the protective tribofilm effect, altering wear behavior.
generation.uncertainty: Other mechanisms (e.g., dynamic recrystallization or local softening) could also contribute, so the exact dominance of the oxide tribofilm can vary with test conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct pin-on-disk tests on FeNiCrCoCu-coated samples at 800–900 °C while varying oxygen partial pressure from near-zero to ambient or above, holding load and sliding velocity constant.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If similar wear and deformation occur irrespective of oxygen partial pressure, the hypothesis that an oxide tribofilm is the dominant controlling mechanism is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 . decision.trend: Earlier studies on high-entropy alloys for elevated-temperature wear (e.g., AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 and CuMoTaWV films) show improved high-temperature tribological performance linked to oxide-based tribofilms. As temperature rises, these self-forming surface oxides can reduce friction and mitigate wear, but the governing mechanism—whether primarily tribofilm nucleation/maintenance or another microstructural process—remains disputed. Despite improved hardness and stable microstructures, clarity is lacking on which single mechanism most directly governs both wear resistance and plastic deformation under sliding at high temperatures.
decision.unsolved: It remains unclear if a protective oxide tribofilm (and its rate of formation) is the overarching controlling factor for wear and microscopic sliding-induced deformation in FeNiCrCoCu coatings at high temperatures, or if other mechanisms such as dynamic recrystallization or high-temperature softening dominate.
decision.lever: Vary the oxygen partial pressure in the test environment (from near-zero to ambient levels) for a baseline FeNiCrCoCu coating at 800–900 °C, and measure changes in oxide film formation, wear rate, friction coefficient, and dislocation structures post-test.
decision.why: If a thermally activated oxide tribofilm governs overall wear resistance and controls near-surface deformation at high temperature, then providing more oxygen (increasing partial pressure) should enhance oxide growth, reduce wear, and modify local dislocation activity. A finding that similar wear behavior occurs regardless of oxygen partial pressure would falsify the hypothesis by showing that the oxide tribofilm is not the primary controlling mechanism.
